article.title: Chicago wrongful convictions
article.author: Michael Steven Smith
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. In October 2026, the Chicago City Council authorized payment via plaintiff Anand. Swaminathan’s law firm Loevy and Loevy of $260.8 million That is over a quarter of $1 billion dollars in compensation for the wrongful murder convictions of the firm’s clients, 17 young men years ago. This settlement against the Chicago Police Department is the largest in the city’s history. They collectively served nearly 400 years in prison for murders for which they were falsely convicted. Attorney Swaminathan and his partner Steve Art litigated their cases for 13 years. The false convictions of murder were arranged by Chicago police detective Reynaldo Guevarra. He was responsible for some 50 convictions, all the frame-ups were accomplishedby using false witness statements, and false coerced confessions. The victims lived in the heavily Latino community of Chicago’s Northwest side in the 1980s and 1990s. The victims are all young men ages 14 to 28. Related: Malcolm X at 100: The Movement for Black Lives Detective Guevara is retired. He lives on a Police Department pension of $91,000 a year and will likely never be held accountable. The passage of time and the unavailability and death of witnesses has so far, got him off the hook. When he was deposed he took the Fifth Amendment some 200 times. Before detective Ronaldo Guevara was sending innocent Latino men to prison, his counterpart Chicago Police Department Commander John Burge was torturing Black men on the southwest side to confess falsely to an array of crimes. This was exposed in litigation and community activism by civil rights attorney Flint Taylor and his law firm the Peoples Law Office. He wrote about it in his book, “The Torture Machine“. With solitary organizing and support, Taylor was able to get a prison sentence for Burge based on perjury. Comedian Lenny Bruce used to say “Chicago is so corrupt it’s thrilling.” Is it possible to reform the police ? What part does racism play? How much money have the citizens of Chicago been forced to pay by the actions of the police department? Will this gargantuan settlement actually bring about reforms? Do the powers that be in Chicago really want reforms? Related: Trump’s Versailles on the Potomac The most fundamental reform would be community control of the police instead of allowing them to terrorize the Black community. Anand Swaminathan grew up in Madison, Wisconsin, the son of immigrant Indian parents who were professors. He attended Harvard law school, where he had more cases in its legal aid efforts than any previous student at the school. Swaminathan is a partner at a law firm of Loevy and Loevy, where he has worked for the last 16 years. Before Swaminathan could sue on behalf of his clients he had to get them he exonerated and released from prison. This was accomplished through the work of Exhonoration Project sponsored by his law firm working with Northwestern University Law School. Overall, this victory and the prior one on police torture would not have happened without the informed and active community in Chicago.
